title: Krishnamoorthi Condemns 240% Surge in Anti-South Asian Hate Posts on X
excerpt: The Illinois Democrat cited a new study counting 542,360 hateful posts targeting South Asians in 18 months, and named a Texas candidate's post and a DHS graphic as examples.
body:
• Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, the Indian American Democrat from Illinois' 8th District, condemned a 240% surge in the monthly volume of anti-South Asian hate posts on X, citing a new Center for the Study of Organized Hate report.
  • The study counted roughly 542,360 hateful posts targeting South Asians between January 2025 and June 2026, with 45% framing South Asians as invaders, job thieves, or a demographic threat.
  • Krishnamoorthi tied the surge to specific episodes: a Texas Republican nominee's post about South Asian students at a University of Texas football game, and a Department of Homeland Security social media graphic featuring a man identified as "Mr. Singh."
  • His message to the community: "South Asian Americans are as much a part of the fabric of America as anyone else, and no amount of hate can erase the contributions we have made to this country."

Indian American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has condemned what he called a surging tide of anti-South Asian hate online, responding to a new study that found a 240% increase in the monthly volume of hateful posts targeting South Asians on X. The Illinois Democrat issued the statement from his office on September 30, urging leaders of both parties to speak out.

The study, titled "The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States" and published by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, counted approximately 542,360 hateful posts targeting South Asians between January 2025 and June 2026. Nearly half — 45% — framed South Asians as invaders, job thieves, or a demographic threat. The researchers pointed to immigration politics, economic resentment, political rhetoric, and digital amplification as drivers. The figures measure online posts, not physical attacks or crimes.

From data to names

Krishnamoorthi did not stop at the aggregate numbers. His statement pointed at two concrete episodes. The first: Bo French, a Texas Republican nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission, posted photos of South Asian students celebrating a University of Texas Longhorns football victory and framed their presence as Americans being "displaced by foreigners." Krishnamoorthi had already condemned that post as racist and xenophobic on September 14, replying to French directly on social media. "These young people were cheering for their university, and he chose to demonise them based solely on how they look," he said at the time.

The second: an official Department of Homeland Security social media post featuring a man identified as "Mr. Singh" in a deportation-themed graphic, which Krishnamoorthi condemned on September 10.

"We have watched politicians demonise South Asians over something as ordinary as attending a college football game and the Trump Administration traffic in racist stereotypes targeting people named Singh."

— Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.)

A bipartisan call

"The 240 per cent surge in monthly anti-South Asian hate on X did not come out of nowhere," Krishnamoorthi said in his September 30 statement. "Americans of every background, and leaders of both parties, need to speak out against racism and xenophobia wherever they appear."

The framing is deliberate: by naming a Republican candidate and a federal agency's own messaging in the same breath as the anonymous online volume, the congressman is making this a fight about political rhetoric from the top — not just trolling in the replies.

Why it matters to the diaspora

For South Asian Americans, the study's numbers put a scale on something many have felt anecdotally: the online environment has measurably worsened, and the hate is increasingly tied to mainstream political narratives about immigration and jobs. Krishnamoorthi's intervention also signals that at least some in Congress see this as a civil-rights issue requiring a public, bipartisan response — not a background condition to be ignored.

"South Asian Americans are as much a part of the fabric of America as anyone else, and no amount of hate can erase the contributions we have made to this country."

— Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.)

What's next

Watch whether other lawmakers — particularly Republicans — join the condemnation, and whether the platforms respond to the study's findings with enforcement changes. The deeper question is whether the rhetoric driving the surge, from campaign accounts to official agency feeds, faces any institutional check.
